english_translation: This year there will be a good harvest, won't there?

dialogue.shona: Gore rino kuchange kuine gohwo rakanaka, handiti?
dialogue.english: This year there will be a good harvest, won't there?
dialogue.literal_gloss: Gore [gore] • rino [rino] • kuchange [to / at change] • kuine [to / at ine] • gohwo [gohwo] • rakanaka [it (past) naka] • handiti [I do not ti]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('rakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'rakanaka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Future with '-cha-' ('kuchange')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kuchange' in this sentence. Whenever you want to say what 'will' happen in the future, simply place the future marker '-cha-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem. For example, 'ndichabika' means 'I will cook', 'tichasvika' means 'we will arrive', and 'mvura ichanaya' means 'the rain will fall'. Pair it with 'mangwana' ('tomorrow') to talk about tomorrow's plans!
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -cha- + Verb Stem = Future ('will') -> Ndichaenda (I will go), Vachadzoka (They will return)

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Gore rino kuchange kuine gohwo rakanaka, handiti?', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

cultural_notes.title: Predicting the Harvest ('Gohwo Rakanaka') & Conversational 'Handiti?'
cultural_notes.content: When the rains fall evenly through December and January, farmers look across green fields of waist-high maize and optimism rises for a strong harvest ('gohwo rakanaka'). Notice 'handiti?' at the end—Shona's universal tag question meaning 'isn't it? / right?'.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Mhepo iri kuvhuvhuta uye mvura ichanaya manheru.'
options: The river is full of water after yesterday's heavy rain.
Tall green trees grow along the sides of the mountain.
The wind is blowing and it will rain in the evening.
The dog barked outside when it saw the visitors.
active_exercises.correct_answer: The wind is blowing and it will rain in the evening.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mhepo iri kuvhuvhuta' = 'The wind is blowing', 'uye' = 'and', 'mvura ichanaya manheru' = 'it will rain in the evening'.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'Tall trees and green grass' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Miti mirefu' = 'tall trees' (plural 'mi-' agreement on '-refu'), and 'neuswa hwegirinhi' = 'and green grass'.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Vana vari kudzidzira kunyora bvunzo kuchikoro.'
options: The children are practicing to write examinations at school.
The teacher gave us new books yesterday morning.
My grandmother grows groundnuts and maize at the rural home.
My friend called me after finishing work today.
active_exercises.correct_answer: The children are practicing to write examinations at school.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vana vari kudzidzira' = 'The children are practicing', 'kunyora bvunzo' = 'to write exams', 'kuchikoro' = 'at school'.
